 SETAF-AF, G-TEAD partner to accelerate counter-drone tech in Africa
 By Capt. Tucker Chase October 16, 2026 
 260430-A-BA877-1034
U.S. Army Pvt. 1st Class David Pomeroy, a combat engineer assigned to the Combat Engineer Company, 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, 173rd Mobile Brigade Combat Team (Airborne), prepares to operate a remote-controlled small ground vehicle equipped with explosive charges during African Lion 26 at Cap Draa, Tan-Tan, Morocco, April 29, 2026. The exercise gave service members an opportunity to test artificial intelligence-powered and autonomous platforms, remote systems, and emerging technologies across attack, defense and mission command operations. The experimentation accelerated target detection, shortened decision timelines and delivered cost-effective warfighting solutions aligned with African partner priorities.
AL26 is U.S. Africa Command's largest annual joint exercise, designed to strengthen collective security capabilities of the U.S., African nations and global allies. Led by U.S. Army Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF) from April 20 to May 8, 2026, and hosted in Ghana, Morocco, Senegal and Tunisia, AL26 involved over 5,600 civilian and military personnel from more than 40 nations, using innovation to drive partner-led regional security.  VICENZA, Italy — U.S. Army Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF) is partnering with the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate to test emerging systems in Africa and deliver them to Soldiers within 180 days.
 The command’s first accelerated capability event, or ACE, is scheduled for spring 2027 in Tan-Tan, Morocco . It will focus on counter-unmanned aircraft systems and force protection, targeting capability gaps in protecting early-entry command posts and operating locations against Group 1–3 small UAS.
 Africa offers an open spectrum, uncongested airspace and diverse terrain that training ranges in the United States and Europe cannot easily match. These conditions allow Soldiers to validate solutions in theater and scale them across the service.

Elijah Edlund, a combat engineer assigned to the Combat Engineer Company, 2nd Battali on, 503rd Infantry Regiment, 173rd Airborne Brigade, mounts a rocket-propelled line charge system onto an autonomous ground platform during African Lion 26 at Cap Draa, Tan-Tan, Morocco, April 30, 2026. The counterattack lane challenged combat engineers to pioneer and validate new tactics, techniques, and procedures for combined arms breaching by integrating robotic and remote systems to reduce obstacles, create standoff and minimize risk to the assault force.

 Operating under the Army Pathway for Innovation and Technology, G-TEAD embeds personnel within Army service component commands. These teams translate urgent commander priorities into executable requirements, giving field commanders access to acquisition authorities at the tactical edge. G-TEAD teams already operate within U.S. Army Europe and Africa, U.S. Army Pacific and U.S. Army Central .
 U.S. Army Col. Christopher Hill, director of G-TEAD, described the organization as the Army's answer for putting innovative solutions in the hands of the warfighter.
 “ASCCs always had priorities, they’ve always had capability gaps, but the two things they’ve never had is acquisition authority and research, development, test and evaluation dollars,” Hill said.
 Hill said that because G-TEAD maintains visibility across multiple commands, its personnel can align modernization efforts, maximize funding and transition proven theater solutions Army wide.
 G-TEAD assigned a team to SETAF-AF in summer 2026 to link immediate operational needs with rapid acquisition resources. Together, the commands will use the ACE framework as a fast-track pathway to identify, evaluate and deliver field-ready technology.
 Through a three-phase model, submission and preparation, Soldier-led demonstrations and follow-on operational evaluation, ACEs deliver rapid solutions within an accelerated acquisition timeline.

 “ACEs are driven by real, urgent, theater-specific technology gaps,” said U.S. Army Maj. Katlin VanWye, a G-TEAD representative embedded with SETAF-AF. “We take commanding general's priorities and translate those immediate tactical challenges into clear, executable technical requirements that defense prize-authority partners and Portfolio Acquisition Executive partners can actually action.”
 SETAF-AF will hold a Soldier-led demonstration in February and March 2027 in Tan-Tan, Morocco, followed by an operational assessment in April and May during African Lion 2027, U.S. Africa Command’s largest joint military exercise in Africa. G-TEAD will validate up to 15 solutions with PAE Fires, one of the U.S. Army’s core modernization enterprises, responsible for shaping, integrating, and delivering the Army’s most critical fires capabilities, as the transition partner.
 An unmanned ground vehicle launches an aerial strike during African Lion 26 at Cap Draa, Tan-Tan, Mo rocco, May 4, 2026. The command field exercise counterattack lane tested new combined arms breach tactics by synchronizing unmanned ground vehicles, remote systems and maneuver elements, demonstrating the integration of autonomous and conventional forces to create standoff, reduce risk and generate new tactical possibilities on the modern battlefield.

 “The ACE is structured around five capability categories,” VanWye said. “An overarching, completely integrated fly‑away kit and four subcategories focused on sUAS detection, kinetic defeat, nonkinetic defeat and passive protection. Solutions will integrate into the Army’s C-UAS command and control Integrated Battle Command System-Maneuver.”
 The initiative supports broader Army modernization priorities while reinforcing partner-led security across the theater.
 U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin R.M. Anderson, commanding general of U.S. Africa Command, and Royal Moroc can Armed Forces Gen. Mohammed Berrid, inspector general of the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces and commander of the Southern Zone, conduct a site visit during African Lion 26 at Cap Draa, Tan-Tan, Morocco, May 8, 2026. The visit brought together senior U.S. and Moroccan military leaders, diplomatic representatives, and coalition partners to reaffirm shared commitments, recognize collective achievements and assess the operational readiness driving AL26's multinational mission.

 “Soldiers need capability,” Hill said. “We have to come in, and we have to actually perform and produce.”
 Hill emphasized that every system receives evaluation with an eye toward scaling across the service, so tactical lessons learned in Africa enhance overall military readiness.
 By accelerating testing and adaptation alongside G-TEAD, SETAF-AF helps provide the joint force with broader strategic options while validating innovative capabilities for the total Army.
